qs.q: What is the main role of an Operating System in a computer system?

c.x: It controls the hardware and coordinates its use among programs
It manages internet connectivity for the user
It compiles the source code of application programs
It supplies electrical power to the hardware

qs.e: The operating system controls the hardware and coordinates its use among the application programs.

qs.q: Which of the following provides basic computing resources such as the CPU, memory, and I/O devices?

c.x: Hardware
Application programs
The operating system
System calls

qs.e: Hardware provides the basic computing resources, while the operating system controls it and application programs use it.

qs.q: What is the main function of application programs in a computer system?

c.x: They define how resources are used to solve user problems
They control the hardware directly at all times
They allocate memory among running processes
They initialize the system when it is powered on

qs.e: Application programs define the ways in which resources are used to solve user problems, unlike the OS which controls the hardware.

qs.q: When the operating system is viewed as a resource allocator, what is its main focus?

c.x: Deciding how resources are allocated among programs and users
Preventing improper use of I/O devices by programs
Compiling and running application source code
Storing user files permanently on secondary storage

qs.e: As a resource allocator, the OS acts as the manager of resources and decides how to allocate them to specific programs and users.

qs.q: When the operating system is viewed as a control program, what is its main focus?

c.x: Deciding which programs receive more memory
Controlling I/O devices and preventing improper use
Scheduling which resources users can purchase
Managing the physical wiring between devices

qs.e: As a control program, the OS controls the I/O devices and manages the execution of user programs to prevent errors and improper use of the computer.

qs.q: Which part of the operating system is the one program that runs at all times?

c.x: The kernel
The system programs
The application programs
The bootstrap program

qs.e: The operating system is made up of the kernel plus system programs, and the kernel is the one program running at all times.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT considered part of, or associated with, the operating system?

c.x: The kernel
The system programs
The application programs
The interrupt handlers

qs.e: The operating system consists of the kernel and system programs, while application programs are not associated with the operating system.

qs.q: In a typical computer system organization, what connects the CPU, device controllers, and memory together?

c.x: The system bus
The kernel
The bootstrap program
The interrupt vector

qs.e: The CPU, disk controller, USB controller, graphics adapter, and memory are all connected through the system bus.

qs.q: What is the main role of a device controller?

c.x: It controls a specific type of connected device
It synchronizes access to shared memory
It decodes instructions fetched by the CPU
It initializes the system when powered on

qs.e: Each device controller controls a specific type of devices, such as a disk controller for disks or a USB controller for USB devices.

qs.q: What is the main role of the memory controller?

c.x: It synchronizes access to the shared memory
It executes application program instructions
It controls printers and other output devices
It stores the interrupt vector permanently

qs.e: The memory controller synchronizes access to the shared memory, while device controllers and the CPU can execute in parallel.

qs.q: What is a bootstrap program?

c.x: A simple program stored in ROM or EEPROM
A large program stored on the hard disk
A user application stored in main memory
A routine stored inside the interrupt vector

qs.e: A bootstrap program is a simple program stored in ROM or EEPROM, also known as firmware.

qs.q: What does the bootstrap program do when the computer is powered up or rebooted?

c.x: It initializes the system and loads the kernel into memory
It manages user files stored on secondary storage
It allocates CPU time among running processes
It handles hardware interrupts during normal operation

qs.e: The bootstrap program initializes all aspects of the system, then locates the kernel, loads it into memory, and starts its execution.

qs.q: What is another common name for the bootstrap program?

c.x: Firmware
Middleware
A device driver
A system call

qs.e: The bootstrap program is also known by the general term firmware.

qs.q: What is an interrupt?

c.x: A signal that is generated when some event occurs
A type of nonvolatile secondary storage device
A fixed memory address used by all programs
A data structure used to store user files

qs.e: An interrupt is a signal that is generated when some event occurs, and each computer architecture has a predefined set of them.

qs.q: A software-generated interrupt that occurs by executing a system call is also known as:

c.x: A trap
A bootstrap
A handler
A controller

qs.e: A software-generated interrupt occurs by executing a system call, and is also called a trap.

qs.q: What distinguishes a hardware-generated interrupt from a software-generated interrupt?

c.x: A hardware interrupt sends a signal to the CPU, a software one runs a system call
A hardware interrupt runs a system call, a software one sends a CPU signal
A hardware interrupt only occurs during bootstrapping of the system
A software interrupt only occurs when the system is powered off

qs.e: A hardware-generated interrupt occurs by sending a signal to the CPU, while a software-generated interrupt (a trap) occurs by executing a system call.

qs.q: What is stored in the interrupt vector?

c.x: The addresses of the interrupt service routines
The contents of all CPU registers
The list of currently running application programs
The data currently held in the system cache

qs.e: The interrupt vector is stored in low memory and holds the addresses of the interrupt service routines (interrupt handlers).

qs.q: When an interrupt occurs, which component is responsible for handling it?

c.x: The interrupt service routine for that interrupt
The bootstrap program stored in ROM
The memory controller of the system
The device controller of any connected device

qs.e: Each interrupt has a corresponding service routine (or handler) that must be executed when that interrupt occurs.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes ROM?

c.x: A storage type whose content cannot be changed
A storage type that can be changed but not often
A volatile storage type used for running programs
A storage type used only for tertiary archiving

qs.e: ROM cannot be changed, unlike EEPROM which can be changed but not frequently.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes EEPROM?

c.x: A storage type whose content can never change
A storage type that can be changed but not often
A volatile storage type used for running programs
A high-speed cache used to hold recent data

qs.e: EEPROM can be changed but not frequently, unlike ROM which cannot be changed at all.

qs.q: What does the CPU's load instruction do?

c.x: It moves a word from RAM to a CPU register
It moves a word from a CPU register to RAM
It moves data from disk directly to cache
It moves data between two locations in RAM

qs.e: The load instruction moves a word from RAM to a CPU register.

qs.q: What does the CPU's store instruction do?

c.x: It moves a word from RAM to a CPU register
It moves the content of a CPU register to RAM
It moves data from disk directly into RAM
It initializes the CPU registers at startup

qs.e: The store instruction moves the content of a CPU register to RAM.

qs.q: What is the correct order of the three main stages of the instruction execution cycle?

c.x: Fetch, then Decode, then Execute
Decode, then Fetch, then Execute
Execute, then Fetch, then Decode
Decode, then Execute, then Fetch

qs.e: The instruction execution cycle proceeds as Fetch, then Decode, then Execute.

qs.q: What happens during the Fetch stage of the instruction execution cycle?

c.x: The instruction is retrieved and stored in the instruction register
The instruction's operands are stored back in memory
The instruction is interpreted and its meaning is determined
The system is initialized and the kernel is located

qs.e: In the Fetch stage, the instruction is fetched from memory and stored in the CPU's instruction register.

qs.q: What happens during the Decode stage of the instruction execution cycle?

c.x: The instruction is interpreted and its operands may be fetched into registers
The instruction is retrieved from memory for the first time
The final result is stored back into main memory
The bootstrap program loads the kernel into memory

qs.e: In the Decode stage, the instruction is decoded, which may require fetching operands from memory and storing them in CPU internal registers.

qs.q: Why do most computer systems need secondary storage in addition to main memory?

c.x: Because main memory is volatile and often too small
Because main memory cannot execute any instructions
Because main memory cannot be reached by the CPU
Because main memory is slower than a hard disk

qs.e: RAM is usually too small to store all needed programs and data, and it is volatile, losing its contents when power is off, so secondary storage is needed.

qs.q: In the storage hierarchy, which type of storage generally has the smallest capacity but the fastest access time?

c.x: Registers
Magnetic tapes
Hard-disk drives
Optical disks

qs.e: In the storage hierarchy, registers sit at the top with the smallest capacity and fastest access time, while tapes sit at the bottom with the largest capacity and slowest access time.

qs.q: Which of the following is classified as tertiary storage in the storage hierarchy?

c.x: Magnetic tapes
CPU registers
The system cache
The main memory

qs.e: Optical disks and magnetic tapes are classified as tertiary storage, while registers, cache, and main memory are primary storage.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of caching in a computer system?

c.x: To hold a copy of recently-accessed data for faster access
To permanently store all of the user's files and data
To increase the total storage capacity of the disk
To control the input and output devices directly

qs.e: Caching refers to the use of high-speed memory to hold a copy of recently-accessed data, assuming it will be needed again soon.

qs.q: What does cache coherency ensure in a computer system?

c.x: An update to cached data is reflected in other copies immediately
All secondary storage devices share the same physical address
The bootstrap program always runs before the kernel loads
Every interrupt is handled by exactly one device controller

qs.e: Cache coherency ensures that an update to some data in a cache is reflected immediately in other caches containing a copy of that data.
